passage:
By Thursday night the community centre’s food-drive room smelled of cardboard, and Vasudha was still labelling boxes at nine. She had come every evening that week, and both weekend days for a month. Her mother had called twice. Her manager had said, gently, that her reports were late.
Kamal, the drive coordinator, found her yawning over a crate. “Go home.”
“I can’t. Who will do the Friday list?”
Guilt twisted in her chest. Slowing down felt like letting people down. Kamal pulled out the rota. “Four of us can share it. You keep Tuesdays and Saturdays.”
Vasudha looked at the rota and, for the first time in weeks, breathed out.

qa.q: How often had Vasudha come to the food-drive room that week?
qa.a: Vasudha had come every evening that week, and both weekend days for a month.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she said she could not go home?
qa.a: She felt guilty and responsible. Slowing down felt to her like letting people down, even though she was worn out.

qa.q: What made Kamal's rota work as a way forward?
qa.a: Kamal shared the tasks among four people and gave Vasudha only two days. That let her keep helping without carrying everything alone.

qa.q: What might Vasudha's mother have been feeling when she called twice that week?
qa.a: Her mother was probably worried and missing her, since Vasudha had hardly been home. The passage only shows the two calls, so it is a guess.

grounding: Shows a committed volunteer whose work and home suffer, who feels guilty about slowing down, and a shared load.

passage:
Dear Mehak,
I’ve written this three times. As the person who runs our youth club rota, you should hear it from me: I need to cut my hours from six days a week to two. I know it feels like walking out on the kids, and I feel guilty even typing it.
Last month I fell asleep at my desk at work, forgot my sister’s birthday dinner, and snapped at a boy who only asked for a football. I keep saying, “I’ll rest after the tournament,” and there is always another tournament.
I’d like to keep the Saturday group and help train two new volunteers so the load isn’t all on me. Could we meet on Monday? I’ll bring a proposal.
Ramesh

qa.q: How many days a week does Ramesh want to work at the youth club?
qa.a: Ramesh wants to cut down from six days a week to two.

qa.q: What is Ramesh feeling while writing the letter?
qa.a: Ramesh feels guilty, since the letter says it feels like walking out on the kids and that typing it brings guilt. Ramesh also seems worn out.

qa.q: What is the wise part of Ramesh's plan?
qa.a: Ramesh keeps the Saturday group and offers to train two new volunteers, so the work is shared. A proposal is promised, not just a complaint.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Mehak may feel worried about the rota but also grateful for the honesty. Ramesh has made it easy to start a plan on Monday.

grounding: Shows a volunteer whose health, work and family suffer, who feels guilty about slowing down and proposes limits and a shared load.

passage: Charu, you asked why I missed your birthday. Honestly, this is Ayesha hitting a wall. For eight months I've been at the animal shelter every evening after work and all weekend. Feeding, cleaning, rescue calls at midnight. I stopped going to the gym, I snapped at Ammi, and my manager warned me about mistakes at work. Every time I thought of taking a day off, I felt like a monster, because who'd feed the puppies? Last week I fell asleep on the shelter floor, and a new volunteer, Divya, found me there at six in the morning. She said, 'You can't carry this alone.' The coordinator made a rota after that. I'm on three evenings now, not seven. I still feel guilty. But I'm sleeping.

qa.q: How many evenings is Ayesha on the rota now?
qa.a: Three evenings, not seven.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel when thinking of taking a day off?
qa.a: Guilty, 'like a monster', worried about who would feed the puppies.

qa.q: What change made Ayesha's service more sustainable?
qa.a: The coordinator's rota, which shared the load so Ayesha now does three evenings instead of every day.

qa.q: How might Divya have felt finding Ayesha on the shelter floor at six in the morning?
qa.a: Worried and concerned, which is why Divya spoke up that Ayesha couldn't carry it alone.

grounding: A committed volunteer gives so much that health, work and family suffer, feels guilty about slowing down, and is helped by a shared rota.

passage: March: Vinita taught at the free evening tuition centre in the basti near her office four nights a week, and loved it. The children called her 'Vinita didi' and waited at the door. June: she was there six nights, plus Sunday planning. She had headaches every day. She missed her cousin's engagement, and her team leader asked if everything was okay. When she thought about cutting down, she pictured little Raju waiting at the door and felt sick with guilt. August: Kavitha, the centre coordinator, sat her down. 'You've been carrying the whole Class 6 batch. That's my mistake as much as yours.' Kavitha found two more volunteers and made a rota. Vinita now teaches two nights. On her first free Wednesday, she slept eleven hours.

qa.q: How many nights does Vinita teach now?
qa.a: Two nights.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel when she thought about cutting down?
qa.a: Sick with guilt, picturing little Raju waiting at the door.

qa.q: How did Kavitha help make Vinita's service sustainable?
qa.a: She admitted the load was unfair, found two more volunteers and made a rota.

qa.q: How might Vinita's team leader have seen her in June?
qa.a: Probably concerned, noticing something was wrong at work, which is why the team leader asked if everything was okay.

grounding: Over months a volunteer takes on so much that work and health suffer, feels guilty about easing off, and is helped by shared load.

passage: Vaibhav, you've been at the food bank every night for two months. Sit, and let your Yamini aunty tell you about 2005. After the floods that year, I worked with a relief group in Mumbai. I thought if I rested, someone would go hungry. I skipped meals, lied to my mother about sleeping, worked sixteen-hour days. One morning I fainted in the warehouse, and a volunteer doctor checked me and sent me home. I cried, not from pain but from guilt. Then our group leader, Farooq bhai, made a rule: no one works more than four days a week. Some people were angry. But the relief work lasted two years instead of two months, because people didn't break. Rest isn't betrayal, beta. It's how the work survives.

qa.q: What rule did Farooq bhai make?
qa.a: No one works more than four days a week.

qa.q: Why did young Yamini cry after being sent home?
qa.a: From guilt, feeling that resting meant letting people down.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the relief work sustainable?
qa.a: Farooq bhai's rule limiting everyone to four days a week, which kept volunteers from breaking and let the work last two years.

qa.q: How might the other volunteers have felt about the four-day rule?
qa.a: Some were angry at first, but it likely saved them from burning out too.

grounding: An aunt recalls burning out as a relief volunteer and how limits and a shared load let the work last.

passage: By Thursday Binita had slept four hours a night for a week. The flood-relief collection drive at the community hall ended on Sunday; her office report was due Friday; her mother had left three voice notes she hadn't played. At 11 p.m. she was still sorting donated blankets, eyes stinging, when her manager emailed: "Second missed deadline this month. Let's talk." Her stomach dropped. Kishore, who ran the drive with her, found her sitting on a pile of blankets. "Go home," he said. "I can't. If I leave, the Friday van won't get loaded." "Then let Rukmini and Faisal load it. They've asked twice." A hot wave of guilt went through her. Handing it over felt like quitting. Kishore sat down beside her. "You're not the drive. You're one of eleven. Let us carry it tomorrow." Slowly she wrote the list for Rukmini, then called her mother back on the walk home.

qa.q: How many voice notes had Binita's mother left?
qa.a: Her mother had left three voice notes.

qa.q: Why did handing over the Friday van feel so hard for Binita?
qa.a: She felt guilty, as if slowing down meant quitting on the people the drive was serving.

qa.q: What did Kishore suggest that could help the work last?
qa.a: Share the load: let Rukmini and Faisal load the van, since she is one of eleven, not the whole drive.

qa.q: How might Rukmini and Faisal feel about finally being handed the task?
qa.a: Having asked twice, they probably feel relieved and trusted to carry part of the work.

grounding: Shows a committed volunteer whose work, sleep and family suffer, who feels guilty slowing down, and who learns to share the load.
